memories.title: ThinkCyber org-account migration strategy
memories.content: For ThinkCyber, prefer ownership/admin transfer over full re-platforming. memories.title: TurboQuant algorithm understanding
memories.content: TurboQuant paper distilled. Core MSE algorithm: normalize vector, apply random orthogonal rotation Pi, exploit coordinate marginal f(x)=Gamma(d/2)/(sqrt(pi)Gamma((d-1)/2))*(1-x^2)^((d-3)/2) on [-1,1], precompute Lloyd-Max scalar codebooks per (d,b), quantize each rotated coordinate independently to nearest centroid, reconstruct via centroid lookup and Pi^T. Core inner-product algorithm: use MSE quantizer at b-1 bits, compute residual r=x-x_mse, store qjl=sign(Sr) with Gaussian S plus gamma=||r||, reconstruct as x_mse + sqrt(pi/2)/d * gamma * S^T qjl to obtain unbiased inner-product estimates. Guarantees: MSE distortion is near-optimal O(4^-b); inner-product distortion is unbiased with variance O(||y||^2/(d 4^b)); lower bounds derived via Shannon lower bound plus Yao minimax. Practical caveats: codebooks depend on d and b, gamma/norm overhead is outside the nominal bit count, and paper proof presentation has minor rigor/presentation quirks but the algorithmic construction is clear and implementation-ready.

memories.title: OpenClaw product wedges: context hydration and OpenClaw-specific QA
memories.content: Research on 2026-03-27 found that OpenClaw has a real but immature extension ecosystem. ClawHub is public/free for skills, so simple skill packs are weak moats. Official docs already cover exec approvals, security audit, OTLP export, OpenProse workflows, and context compaction; a community plugin (LinkMind Context Engine) already offers remote compression. The strongest monetizable wedges are (1) a cross-session knowledge/context hydration product that solves MEMORY.md limitations and compaction pain, and (2) an OpenClaw-specific reliability/eval product for skills/plugins, since official testing docs say skill-focused decisioning/compliance/workflow-contract evals are still missing. Private registry/provenance for teams is a high-moat but slower enterprise path.

memories.title: AI workflow products: sell outcomes, not templates
memories.content: As of 2026-03-27, the market for AI workflows is real but generic workflow templates are increasingly commoditized. Official signals: Zapier says over 3.4 million businesses use its automation platform and offers AI starter kit templates; n8n exposes 8,700+ workflow templates and an AI Workflow Builder that constructs workflows from natural language. The defensible product is an outcome-specific workflow kit with schemas, examples, validations, evals, and fallback/human review, not an n8n JSON export alone. Best target for semi-passive income is technical-adjacent operators with well-defined, measurable tasks such as support triage, lead intake, meeting-to-CRM, or document extraction.

memories.title: Urgent cash strategy: services before products
memories.content: When a user needs approximately  within 7-10 days and has technical skills but limited budget, the primary recommendation should be a narrow productized service sold with upfront payment. Digital products and passive-income bets are secondary because discovery and payout timing are slower; current marketplace friction includes Fiverr taking 20% and standard withdrawal after a 14-day clearance, Gumroad requiring at least a 7-day payout period with first-payout review, while Upwork and Contra are more viable for client-brought contracts but still add platform friction.

memories.title: Claude Code Opus 1M rate-limit diagnosis 2026-03-26
memories.content: On 2026-03-26 America/Los_Angeles, Claude Code Pro auth was healthy but default config model=opus[1m] caused immediate synthetic rate_limit failures. Live probes showed: default (opus[1m]) -> API Error: Rate limit reached; opus[1m] + medium -> still fails; opus + high -> succeeds; sonnet + medium -> succeeds. Root cause is the saved 1M-context Opus model hitting a model-specific capacity/quota gate, not general login failure. Fix applied in ~/.claude/settings.json: change model from opus[1m] to opus and keep effortLevel high. Note: usage bar can still show about 50 percent because that is not the same as the model-specific short-term limit.

memories.title: Noesis runtime path is daemon-first with local read fallback
memories.content: The main runtime path in /Users/dominion/noesis is CLI -> NoesisClient -> JSON-RPC over Unix socket -> daemon handlers backed by SQLite schema v3 and cognitive stores. When IPC is unavailable, runtime/local-rpc.ts provides a snapshot-based local fallback for read operations and blocks protected writes. This split-trust design is central to how recall, explanation, and some cognitive reads still work in sandboxed environments while persistent writes require trusted access.

memories.title: MiniMax M2.5 NIM tool call newline stripping root cause
memories.content: Root cause: vLLM minimax_m2_tool_parser.py line 197 calls param_match.group(2).strip() which strips ALL leading/trailing whitespace including newlines from XML parameter values. MiniMax official manual parsing guide also strips leading/trailing newlines explicitly. This is by design in the parser, not a bug per se - the XML format puts newlines between tags and values. The real issue is that for multi-line content (like code), Python .strip() removes meaningful newlines. SGLang uses same pattern. NVIDIA NIM hosted API (build.nvidia.com/integrate.api.nvidia.com) has NO user-configurable tool parser - it runs a fixed backend. Self-hosted NIM containers support NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN but LLM-specific NIMs auto-configure and docs warn against setting tool calling env vars. vLLM issue 28963 is about AttributeError in type conversion, not newline stripping. SGLang issue 16057 is about OR vs AND logic in null type checking, not newlines.

memories.title: MiniMax M2.5 tool calling research
memories.content: MiniMax M2.5 uses XML-based tool calling format with <minimax:tool_call><invoke name='fn'><parameter name='key'>value</parameter></invoke></minimax:tool_call>. Known bugs: vLLM parser crashes on list-type param_type, SGLang parser fails on anyOf/null union types, OpenClaw sub-agents drop required parameters. Multi-line strings are stripped of leading/trailing newlines by parser. Recommended: use vLLM or SGLang with built-in parsers, or OpenAI SDK compatibility layer. NVIDIA NIM hosts M2.5 as minimaxai/minimax-m2.5 with 204800 token context. Alternative NIM models with strong tool calling: Llama 3.1/3.2/3.3, Mistral, Nemotron Nano/Super/Ultra, Qwen 3.5, GLM-4.7.

memories.content: Sandboxed agents can now use Noesis read and intelligence paths through automatic local fallback: recall, check, and orchestrate-style context assembly no longer depend on daemon IPC. Persistent write operations are intentionally kept on the trusted path and still require real access to ~/.agents so audit logging, signing, and durable storage are preserved. memories.title: Noesis recall sandbox fallback and pinned runtime
memories.content: Sandboxed agents cannot use daemon IPC against ~/.agents/daemon.sock and SQLite cannot safely query ~/.agents/noesis.db in place because the sandbox blocks lock-side effects. Recall now falls back to a temp snapshot copy of noesis.db plus optional -wal/-shm sidecars, then runs local retrieval against that snapshot with access-metadata writes disabled. The CLI entrypoint is pinned to /opt/homebrew/bin/node instead of env node so agents in different working directories do not hit Node ABI drift with better-sqlite3.

memories.title: Noesis daemon IPC blocked in sandboxed runtimes
memories.content: Root cause: sandboxed agent processes can receive EPERM when connecting to ~/.agents/daemon.sock even when the Noesis daemon is healthy and listening. In this environment, socket listen/connect is blocked by sandbox policy, and direct write access to ~/.agents/noesis.db is also restricted, so daemon-backed Noesis commands must run outside the sandbox or via an explicit noesis allowlist. Status should not infer daemon health from socket-file presence alone.

memories.title: Noesis HMAC signing uses pre-generated ULID
memories.content: The write pipeline must generate the ULID before computing the HMAC signature, and pass that same ID to createMemory. If createMemory generates its own ID, the stored ID will not match the signed ID, causing all HMAC verification to fail on recall. This was a critical bug that caused every memory to appear tampered.

memories.title: TypeScript ONNX integration pattern
memories.content: When integrating ONNX Runtime with TypeScript for embedding models, use WordPiece tokenization from the HuggingFace tokenizer.json file rather than hash-based tokenization. Hash-based tokenization produces random token IDs that are meaningless to the model and result in garbage embeddings. Proper WordPiece subword splitting gives cosine similarity above 0.8 for semantically related texts.
